column11: Megillah 13a: ‘The Gemara explains how all the names in fact are referring to Moses: “Jered”; this is Moses, and why was he called Jered? column11: Chagigah 10a: ‘MISHNA: Incidental to the Festival peace-offering, the mishna describes the nature of various areas of Torah study. The halakhot of the dissolution of vows, when one requests from a Sage to dissolve them, fly in the air and have nothing to support them, as these halakhot are not mentioned explicitly in the Torah. There is only a slight allusion to the dissolution of vows in the Torah, which is taught by the Sages as part of the oral tradition.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 10a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this is the "hovering in the air," after the manner stated in Chagigah (10a): "The dissolution of vows hovers in the air and has nothing to lean upon"; Rashi explaining: it derives from the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And this is likewise true, harmonizing completely with the Talmudic exposition; and see there that they interpreted "the instruments of a foolish shepherd" as referring to the slave dynasty of Herod, which roots in the mystery of Solomon's servants explained above (folio 40b), when the royal crown was wrested from Priesthood to Monarchy under Alexander Yannai, the first to be titled king, at which time the Sages said to him: "Let the crown of priesthood suffice for you, etc." (Kiddushin 66a).
column15: And whoever stubbornly insists on acting in lawless expansion without conscious restraint, relying antinomian-style on the premise that the Blessed Name brings everything into being — concerning this the Midrash and Talmud state (Chagigah 16a): the Holy One says, “It is not My wish that My Name be mentioned upon a dunghill.”

column11: Chagigah 10a: ‘Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said: If I had been there, sitting with those Sages, I would have said to them: My source is better than yours, as it is stated: “He shall not nullify his word” (Numbers 30:3), from which it may be inferred: He himself cannot nullify his word; however, others, i.e., a Sage, may nullify it for him by dissolving his vow. Rava said: For all of the suggested sources for the dissolution of vows there is a possible refutation, except for that of Shmuel, for which there is no refutation.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 10a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And the intention of this "faint hint" does not refer to the scriptural derivations cited in the Gemara: "he shall not break his word—he cannot dissolve, but others can dissolve for him," and the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: “That the willful sins become as inadvertent ones or as merits” — and this is the rectification of the past, in deeds that have already emerged into act. [kashalta] in your iniquity’ (Hoshea 14:2) — ‘iniquity’ is willful, yet it is called a ‘stumbling’ [inadvertent]. But Reish Lakish [also] said: Great is teshuvah, for willful sins become for him as merits, as it says, ‘and when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, by them he shall live’ (Yechezkel 33:19)! — It is not difficult: here [merits] from love, there [inadvertent] from fear.” R’ Tzadok builds the whole siman on this ahavah/yirah distinction.).
column15: And the Flood generation expanded in their attributes without limit, an expansive power belonging to no creature, but exclusively to Hashem. For every created entity is composed of two opposing, polar elements; as in Zohar Toldot (136b): Everything created by the Holy One, except for Himself, is formed in partnership; even the celestial hosts: although angels have no dense physical body, they cannot act until the holy soul is partnered with them —.

column11: Menachot 29b: ‘§ Rav Yehuda says that Rav says: When Moses ascended on High, he found the Holy One, Blessed be He, sitting and tying crowns on the letters of the Torah. Moses said before God: Master of the Universe, who is preventing You from giving the Torah without these additions? God said to him: There is a man who is destined to be born after several generations, and Akiva ben Yosef is his name; he is destined to derive from each and every thorn of these crowns mounds upon mounds of halakhot. It is for his sake that the crowns must be added to the letters of the Torah.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Menachot 29b) to illuminate his exposition here (“but merely an ethereal allusion within the crowns of the letters which Rabbi Akiva expounded (Menachos 29b); for just as the Sages stated (Bamidbar Rabbah 18:21): on the Tablets of the Covenant,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: This explains what the Sages said in Menachot 29b, that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not understand the words of Rabbi Akiva; and in Midrash Rabbah (Chukat) that “Rabbi Akiva’s eye saw what Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not see.” Though none arose like Moses, this refers specifically to attainment through visionary sight, for to Moses was revealed everything an advanced student would ever innovate, even what Rabbi Akiva would innovate.
column15: In truth, sin and punishment are one identical reality, as expounded in Midrash Rabbah on Lamentations 3:38: “Out of the mouth of the Most High proceed not evil and good,” appearing as separate matters only before human mortal eyes.

column11: Bamidbar Rabbah 18:21: ‘Mem, nun, tzadi, peh, kaf, the double letters, were stated by the prophets. Kaf kaf alludes to Abraham: “Lekh lekha” (Genesis 12:1) – he will beget a son at the age of one hundred. is for Isaac: “For you have grown much mightier than we [mimenu]” (Genesis 26:16). He alluded to him that he and his descendants would be mighty in two worlds. Nun nun for Jacob: “Deliver me, please [hatzileni na]” (Genesis 32:12); deliver in two worlds. Peh peh to Israel, [when God said] to Moses: “I have remembered you [pakod pakadeti]” (Exodus 3:16). Tzadi tzadi – “Behold a man, Tzemaḥ is his name, [and he will sprout [yitzmaḥ…]” (Zechariah 6:12). And it says: “I will establish for David a righteous offshoot [tzemaḥ tzadik] and he will reign as king and succeed, and he will perform justice and righteousness in the land” (Jeremiah 23:5).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bamidbar Rabbah 18:21) to illuminate his exposition here (“for just as the Sages stated (Bamidbar Rabbah 18:21): on the Tablets of the Covenant, between each commandment were inscribed all the detailed mitzvos of the Torah; so within the Written Torah,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Meaning within the scholar who heads the community of Israel in that era like Moses, into whom Moses' illumination directly radiates, as does the light of all past leaders, just as the collective generation bears the light of King David derived from the verse "I remembered," and so on throughout all generations as explained.
column15: “And I, behold, I establish My covenant with you, and with your seed after you.” In the sealing of this covenant with the sons of Noah it is not written “for perpetual generations” (le-dorot olam), as it is written concerning Abraham our Father (Genesis 17:7): “And I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your seed after you in their generations for an everlasting covenant.”

column11: Taanit 9a: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan sat down and wondered aloud about this verse, saying: Is there anything that is written in the Writings that is not alluded to in the Torah at all? I cannot think of any hint of this idea in the Torah itself. The child said to him: Is that to say that this idea is really not alluded to in the Torah? But isn’t it written, with regard to Joseph’s brothers: “And their heart failed them and they turned trembling to one to another, saying: What is this that God has done to us?” (Genesis 42:28). This verse exemplifies the notion that when one sins and encounters troubles, he wonders why it is happening to him.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 9a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and everything that a veteran disciple is destined to innovate, for there is nothing that is not hinted in the Torah; all is hinted within the intervening air, within the tagin and crowns of the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And when they judge capital cases and penalties to execute and punish transgressors, you might have thought that they impart a wrathful heart, anger, and murderous impulse into the generation. Regarding this they declared: 'Our hands did not shed,' meaning: we did not, Heaven forbid, draw down an impulse of bloodshed into the generation.
column15: And in the Jerusalem Talmud (Ta'anit 1:2): Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: “‘And a mist went up from the earth’—when brokenness ascends from below, immediately the rains descend.”

column11: Kiddushin 66a: ‘The Gemara interjects: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says: Immediately, heresy was injected into Yannai, as he should have said to Elazar ben Po’ira: This works out well with regard to the Written Torah, as it can be studied by all on their own, but what will become of the Oral Torah? The Oral Torah is transmitted only by the Sages. The baraita continues: Immediately, the evil arose and caught fire through Elazar ben Po’ira, and all the Sages of the Jewish people were killed. And the world was desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shataḥ came and restored the Torah to its former glory. This completes the baraita.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 66a) to illuminate his exposition here (“wherefore the Written Torah is written and laid open for all who enter the world (Kiddushin 66a); whereas the Oral Torah is that which was entrusted unto the Sages to innovate and grasp, each...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column12: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 5:4 (§3)
column13: And many other teachings, wherein they disclosed in the Oral Torah that which was concealed in the Written Torah concerning converts. For from the perspective of the Written Torah—which is the transcendent Torah of Hashem—it lies placed in a corner, and whoever wishes may come and take it [Kiddushin 66a]; but regarding the Oral Torah, what can be said?, as the Gemara states in Kiddushin [ibid.].
column15: And this is why the Midrash compares White Fire to the parchment, and Black Fire to the written ink. For parchment represents the undifferentiated totality enclosing all Torah concepts, whereas letters define and channel the infinite light; since every letter possesses its own specific border so man can grasp its light, and this division into particulars is the text defining limits: “this you may eat, and this you may not eat.”

column11: Numbers 30:3: ‘If anyone makes a vow to GOD or takes an oath imposing an obligation on themselves, they shall not break their pledge; they must carry out all that has crossed their lips.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Numbers 30:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“and if so, the prohibition does not stem from human wisdom, but from the Torah which decreed: "he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth; he shall not break his word" (Bamidbar...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And even if one intended to commit a prohibited act, but permitted matter happened into his hand (Nazir 23a) — such as pork and lamb meat lying before him, and he intended to eat the pork, but lamb meat came up in his hand — he requires forgiveness and atonement; as it is stated (Numbers 30:13): "her husband has made them void; and Hashem will forgive her" — even though her husband annulled her vow, since she was unaware of his annulment and ate — "Hashem will forgive her" implies she requires forgiveness and atonement.
column15: And all this divine wisdom decreed—constricting His light so that free will might exist, enabling man to serve Hashem in the aspect of a servant (eved) as well as a child (ben). For a son does not tremble lest he acted contrary to his father's will, knowing his father looks favorably upon him; being naturally inclined toward his father's pleasure, he is confident he aligned with his wishes.

column11: Bekhorot 36b: ‘§ Rav Yehuda says that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says the following halakha, but he was uncertain whether Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said it in the name of Rav and uncertain whether he said it in the name of Shmuel: Three regular Jews may permit a firstborn animal with clear-cut blemishes in a place where there is no expert. The Gemara asks: What is Rav Yehuda teaching us by this statement? We already learn this in the mishna: That animal may be slaughtered on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bekhorot 36b) to illuminate his exposition here (“whereas the dissolution depends upon wisdom, having been committed unto the Sages: exclusively an ordained expert (yachid mumcheh) or three laymen (Bechoros 36b); who constitute a rabbinical court...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Whereas in the wisdom of Rabbi Akiva, representing the Oral Torah, ultimate validation occurs only when Hashem illuminates his eyes that this ruling corresponds to the Halachah of Moses from Sinai, as the Sages stated: "Whatever a seasoned scholar will innovate in the future was already spoken to Moses at Sinai"; meaning that it is authentic wisdom [finding its intimation in the Written Torah, for nothing lacks an allusion in the Torah of Moses], meaning that he perceives and knows with certainty that his insight is indeed a Halachah given to Moses at Sinai, representing the authentic innovation of a seasoned scholar.
column15: Whereas an animal, which possesses neither higher spiritual life nor moral choice—its vitality being merely ephemeral, never having committed sin—cannot be summoned at all by necromancy. And prior to the Flood, the Blessed Name did not permit man to eat of living flesh, because the animal kingdom was in a state of natural perfection, having never deviated from the divine Will.

column11: Sanhedrin 3a: ‘The Gemara asks: Is that to say that with three judges they will not be among those who sit idly on street corners? How is this concern addressed by increasing the number of judges? The Gemara answers: When there are three judges it is impossible, i.e., highly unlikely, that there is not among them one who is learned. The Gemara asks: If that is so, then if they err they should not be liable to pay compensation, since rabbinic law authorizes laymen to judge cases of this nature. The Gemara answers: If the judges will be exempt from paying compensation in the event that they err in their judgment, this lack of accountability will lead all the more so to having many of those who sit idly on street corners assume the role of judges.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 3a) to illuminate his exposition here (“who constitute a rabbinical court for all judicial matters, it being impossible that at least one of them is not learned (Sanhedrin 3a); they possessing wisdom, dissolution depending upon the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Moreover, the latter clause, "I will heal your backslidings" [in Yirmiyah, addressed in the second person], refers to [teshuvah] from fear — and there is no complete healing, only "a trace of his name remains"; whereas the healing [spoken of] in Hoshea ["I will heal their backsliding, loving them freely"] is complete. asks the same controlling question: if teshuvah from fear has secured pardon, what remains in calling the former willful sins shegagos? His answer throughout these teachings is that fear removes the rebellious will but leaves the deed’s residual form; love reaches the root and transforms the past.
column15: And this is “if you do well, se'et”—you shall be elevated above your brother, having endured many constrictions. “And if you do not well, sin crouches at the door”—meaning: if you do not refine yourself now and wait until the threshold of the grave, there you can no longer refine yourself, for there sin crouches, it being impossible to separate it from the heart as one can in this world.

column11: Genesis 11:4: ‘And they said, “Come, let us build us a city, and a tower with its top in the sky, to make a name for ourselves; else we shall be scattered all over the world.”’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Genesis 11:4) to illuminate his exposition here (“and so the tower of the Generation of Dispersion (Bereishis 11:4); and Lamed signifies learning (limud), whence derives the study and sustenance of the Oral Torah; and "the words of the Scribes...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: The three factions of the Generation of the Dispersion correspond to the three heads of evil: Those who said "Let us ascend and dwell there" denied the Root, claiming no Sovereign sits enthroned there. And those who said "Let us ascend and wage war" rebelled against the Supreme, embodying Keter of the Sitra Achra.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:5 (§2)
column15: Allowing them to expand in willful lust upon that false security. "And from there Hashem scattered them" (Genesis 11:8)— meaning: what value is this peace that you forged among yourselves?! And although it is a great matter that My Name is called Peace, as in the Talmud (Shabbat 10b), yet your entire design is that through this you erase My Name!

column11: Avodah Zarah 35a: ‘§ The mishna teaches that Rabbi Yehoshua diverted Rabbi Yishmael’s attention to another matter, and began discussing the verse: “For your love is better than wine” (Song of Songs 1:2). The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the verse: “For your love [dodekha] is better than wine”? When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, he said: The congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: Master of the Universe, the statements of Your beloved ones [dodekha], i.e., the Sages, are more pleasant to me than the wine of the written Torah itself.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 35a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "the words of the Scribes are more beloved than the wine of the Torah" (Avodah Zarah 35a; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2); for the Written Torah is prophetic perception through a supreme prophet...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: For the entire world was created for the sake of Israel, and for the sake of the Torah, called reishis”; the midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 36:4) likewise teaches that the world endures in the merit of Israel. R’ Tzadok’s use: because the world thus “belongs” to Israel, its abundance is theirs to elevate — to “absorb the power of holiness that sustains it and brings it into being”; but should they sink into it as an end in itself, they sever both it and themselves from its Source., [and so] it has a “belonging” to them.
column15: And following the collapse of the Dispersion, Abraham became master in words of Torah, permanent holiness being established within him, Hashem sealing His covenant of Torah upon him, such that whatever he performed was aligned with the divine Will, transcending even the preparatory derech eretz that preceded the Torah; as elucidated in Mei HaShiloach (Vol. 1, Noach, s.v. Vayihyu Yemei Terach) on Bereishit Rabbah 39:7: “The Holy One said to Abraham: You I exempt from honoring father and mother, but I do not exempt another from honoring father and mother” (examine there).

column11: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2: ‘Another matter, “as your love is better than wine”—matters of Torah were analogized to water, to oil, to honey, and to milk. To water, “ho, everyone who is thirsty, go to water” (Isaiah 55:1); just as water [extends] from one end of the earth to the other, as it is written: “To the One who spreads the earth over the water” (Psalms 136:6), so too, Torah, [extends] from one end of the earth to the other, as it is stated: “Its measure is longer than the earth” (Job 11:9). Just as water provides life to the world, as it is stated: “A garden spring, a well of living water” (Song of Songs 4:15), so too, Torah provides life to the world, as it is stated: “They are life for those who find them” (Proverbs 4:22), and it is written: “Go, purchase and eat” (Isaiah 55:1).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "the words of the Scribes are more beloved than the wine of the Torah" (Avodah Zarah 35a; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2); for the Written Torah is prophetic perception through a supreme prophet...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And even though it was destroyed, nonetheless Shlomo’s words were recorded, that he said of himself, “I have built a house [of habitation for You],” because the first holiness “sanctified for the Future,” and it is destined to return and be rebuilt, and the nullification was only for a time. And had David built it, it truly would not have been destroyed; only that his enemies, who said “evil to him,” caused that his holiness was not revealed in actuality in this world in his days, and through this he did not merit to build it.
column15: For just as in the body the physical hand and foot are garments for the inner hand and foot of the soul, which act through words of Torah— one receiving Torah wisdom and the other bestowing it upon another—so every generation is a garment for the one that succeeds it.

column11: Bava Batra 12a: ‘Ameimar said: And a Sage is greater than a prophet, as it is stated: “And a prophet has a heart of wisdom” (Psalms 90:12), i.e., he is wise. When comparisons are drawn, who is compared to whom? You must say that the lesser is compared to the greater. Here too, prophecy is compared to wisdom, thus indicating that wisdom is greater than prophecy. Abaye said: Know that this is so, that the Sages still enjoy the prophetic gift, as a great man makes a statement with regard to a point of halakha and the same statement is then cited in the name of a different great man in accordance with his statement, indicating that the Sages makes their statements by way of prophecy.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 12a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for the Written Torah is prophetic perception through a supreme prophet like Moshe Rabbeinu, yet "a sage is superior to a prophet" (Bava Batra 12a); for the sage grasps through the Holy Spirit...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Although prophecy is an explicit revelation of visions of Hashem far beyond the intellectual perception of the sages, nevertheless the Sages taught in Bava Batra 12a that “a sage is superior to a prophet”; and see Nachmanides there, who explains that the sage can attain greater depths. And as is known from the holy Ari of blessed memory, who disclosed teachings concerning supernal worlds which by his own reckoning transcend the attainment of all the prophets.
column15: And in humanity one soul never tasted death: Elijah the Prophet. Thus within all distant, fallen realms a single indestructible point remains. So in divine service: where intent appears far removed from Hashem, a hidden, pure spark remains in the heart, from which supreme goodness ultimately sprouts.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 17:5: ‘“The Lord God cast a deep slumber upon the man, and he slept. He took one of his sides, and He closed it with flesh in its place [taḥtena]” (Genesis 2:21). “The Lord God cast [hipil] a deep slumber” – Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of Rabbi Levi: The beginning of downfall [mapala] is sleep. When a person sleeps, he does not toil in Torah and does not do any work. literally means, “He caused to fall down.” Rav said: There are three slumbers: the slumber of sleep, the slumber of prophecy, and the slumber of a trance. The slumber of sleep – “the Lord God cast a deep slumber upon the man, and he slept.” The slumber of prophecy – “it was when the sun was setting, and a deep slumber fell upon Abram” (Genesis 15:12).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 17:5) to illuminate his exposition here (“for the sage grasps through the Holy Spirit from supernal holiness the supreme Chochmah which transcends the Written Torah (which is merely the fallen fruit of higher wisdom, Bereishis Rabbah...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And deep slumber (tardemah) is succumbing to sleep [and see Bereishit Rabbah 17 where it signifies profound torpor]. And "summer" (kayitz) and "harvest" (katzir) parallel the two Talmudic formulations in Eruvin (13b) that one must "scrutinize" (yefashpesh) and "examine" (yemasmesh) his deeds: "harvest" is scrutinizing during the act, while "summer" is examining retrospectively after the deed.
column15: In truth, prior to the Blessed Name beginning to bestow, man did not feel any deficiency or constriction whatsoever; however, when the Blessed Name begins to illuminate Chochmah within man—such that he begins to see that every detail is directed by the Blessed Name, yet the light has not yet shone upon him fully—man possesses only an inkling from this illumination.

column11: Deuteronomy 13:1: ‘Be careful to observe only that which I enjoin upon you: neither add to it nor take away from it.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 13:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“being the word of Hashem to which nothing can be added or diminished (Devarim 13:1), which are measured, fixed, and enduring words; while from another vantage the Holy Spirit of the sages of the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column12: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, On Mitzvot 7:1 (§3)
column13: And see Tosafot in Eruvin [100a, s.v. Matan], who challenged: Why should not the positive command of applying four blood applications upon the altar override the negative prohibition of "Do not add" (bal tosif [Deuteronomy 13:1])? And they resolved: it is not analogous to diverse fibers (sha'atnez) in tzitzit, for here the entanglement came about through his own negligence, and he could have fulfilled the mitzvah without overriding the prohibition; thus far their words.
column15: So it was before creation: gazing at the light with measured reverence was sublime mitzvah, while gazing unchecked was forbidden, turning Hei into Chet. And one who refused to perceive the light altogether turned “do not profane” into “do not praise,” withholding due glory and ruining creation; for the Blessed Name ordained gazing with measured discipline—neither rushing recklessly forward nor turning entirely away.

column11: Sefer Yetzirah 6:3: ‘Three, but each one stands alone. 7 divided: Three opposite Three, with an edict deciding between them. Twelve stand in war: Three Friends, Three Foes, Three Lifegivers, and Three Executioners. Three Friends: the heart and the ears and the mouth. Three foes: the liver and the gall and the tongue. And EL, the faithful king, rules over them all: One over Three, Three over Seven, Seven over Twelve, and all of them fastened this one to that one.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 12, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Sefer Yetzirah 6:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“which matches "the heart is king over the body" as written in Sefer Yetzirah (6:3); and "Malchus is the mouth, the Oral Torah we call it," as written at the start of Tikkun 17 (Tikkunei Zohar);...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And it is stated there, in the matter of Michah — and likewise at the start of the account of the children of Dan afterward — “in those days there was no king in Israel” (Shoftim 17:6; 18:1)” — “in those days there was no king in Israel” (17:6 adds: “each man did what was right in his own eyes”). Background: the refrain of Sefer Shoftim’s closing chapters, framing an age of disorder before the monarchy. column11: Avodah Zarah 9a: ‘In relation to the discussion on the calculation of years, the Gemara states that one of the Sages of the school of Eliyahu taught: The world is destined to exist for six thousand years. The last set of two thousand years are the period designated for the days of the Messiah, but due to our many sins there are those years that have been taken from them, i.e., such and such years have already passed and have been taken from the two thousand years that are designated for the Messiah, and the Messiah has not yet arrived.
